message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
I think this post-mortem is a good example of the team diagnosing a problem properly rather than guessing. We had a clean natural experiment: the Reorder button was removed on 2 February and restored on 2 March with nothing else changing, and orders per user fell and then recovered in step with it, corroborated by a tenfold rise in support contacts about reordering. We quantified the damage carefully, at 39,600 lost orders and roughly £1.05 million in revenue, so leadership can see the real cost. The platform breakdown also helps target the fix, since it shows Android users were hit hardest, consistent with the deeper menu placement on that build. We were also careful not to throw out the good parts of v5.0: the data show search-bar users order 40% more, which gives us a clear direction for v5.2. The actions are concrete, owned and measurable, and they address both the testing gap and the monitoring gap. I am confident we understand what happened and have the right changes in place.
</author>

Your review is being evaluated on whether it identifies the problems in the document.

<document>
Post-mortem: Larder App v5.0 Navigation Redesign
Product team, 20 March 2026 (blameless format)

Summary
On 2 February 2026 we released v5.0 of the Larder grocery app on iOS and Android, replacing the five-tab bottom navigation with a three-tab layout and a persistent search bar. Weekly orders fell sharply in the following weeks. We identified the removal of the Reorder button from the home screen as the main cause and restored it in v5.0.3 on 2 March, after which orders recovered to close to pre-release levels. This document sets out what happened, what we learned and what we will change.

What changed in v5.0
- Bottom navigation reduced from five tabs (Home, Browse, Search, Orders, Account) to three (Home, Browse, Account), with search moved to a persistent bar at the top of every screen.
- The Reorder button, which let customers repeat a previous order with one tap from the home screen, moved into Account > Order history.
- A new recipe-led home feed.
The release passed our standard usability testing with 12 participants, all of whom were new users recruited through a research panel. No existing customers were included.

Impact
Table 1. Weekly active users (WAU) and orders
Week starting | WAU | Orders | Orders per WAU
19 Jan | 48,200 | 61,700 | 1.28
26 Jan | 48,600 | 62,200 | 1.28
2 Feb (v5.0 released) | 47,900 | 55,100 | 1.15
9 Feb | 46,800 | 51,500 | 1.10
16 Feb | 46,300 | 50,900 | 1.10
23 Feb | 46,100 | 50,700 | 1.10
2 Mar (v5.0.3, Reorder restored) | 46,400 | 56,600 | 1.22
9 Mar | 47,000 | 59,700 | 1.27

Between the two pre-release weeks (average 61,950 orders) and the three weeks from 9 to 23 February (average about 51,030), weekly orders fell by about 10,900, or 18%. Orders per active user fell from 1.28 to 1.10, while WAU fell only about 4%, which told us that customers were still opening the app but not completing orders.

Across the four weeks from 2 to 23 February, we estimate that 39,600 orders were lost relative to the pre-release baseline. At our average order value of £38, this is approximately £1.05 million in lost revenue.

Table 2. Change in weekly orders by platform, pre-release vs 9-23 February
Platform | Share of WAU | Change in orders
iOS | 58% | -21%
Android | 42% | -13%

The decline was concentrated among Android users, which is consistent with the Android build placing order history one level deeper in the Account menu than the iOS build does.

Root cause
Session recordings and support tickets both pointed to the Reorder button. Support contacts mentioning "reorder", "repeat order" or "last order" rose from about 40 a week to 410 in the week of 9 February. Roughly 45% of pre-release orders had been placed through Reorder, and the new path to it required four taps instead of one. When v5.0.3 restored the button to the home screen on 2 March, orders per user recovered to 1.22 that week and 1.27 the following week, close to the pre-release 1.28. The timing of both the fall and the recovery, and the absence of any other change in v5.0.3, make us confident in this diagnosis.

Detection
The drop was visible in the daily orders dashboard on 3 February, but nobody was watching orders per user as a release metric, and the first escalation came on 10 February. The rollback decision was then delayed while we prepared a fix rather than reverting.

What went well
The persistent search bar has been a success. Customers who used the new search bar at least once in a week placed 40% more orders that week than customers who did not. Search is clearly driving purchasing, and we will build on this by making search results the default landing view for returning users in v5.2.

What we will change
1. Usability tests for changes to existing flows will include at least six existing customers, weighted towards frequent buyers.
2. Any release that moves an element used in more than 10% of orders will be staged to 10% of users for a week, with orders per WAU as a guardrail metric.
3. An automated alert will fire when orders per WAU falls more than 5% week on week.
4. For regressions in core purchase flows, the default response will be to revert first and fix afterwards.

Conclusion
The incident was caused by moving a heavily used shortcut without testing with the customers who relied on it, and was prolonged by weak release monitoring. Both are fixable, and the actions above address them directly.
</document>
response:
# Review: Larder App v5.0 Navigation Redesign Post-mortem

The diagnosis of the Reorder button is reasonably supported. However, the revenue figure is wrong by about £450k, the platform finding is reversed, and the search-bar conclusion is weakly evidenced and points v5.2 back toward the same mistake. Several of your summary claims don't hold up against the document itself.

## Factual and arithmetic errors

**1. Lost revenue is about £1.5 million, not £1.05 million.**
- The 39,600 lost orders figure is correct. Against the 61,950 baseline, the weekly shortfalls are 6,850 + 10,450 + 11,050 + 11,250.
- But 39,600 × £38 = **£1,504,800**. The document understates the cost to leadership by about £450k. Since you cite this figure as the "real cost", it must be fixed.

**2. The platform conclusion contradicts Table 2.**
- The table shows **iOS** fell 21% and **Android** 13%. The text says the decline was "concentrated among Android users".
- The weighted figures check out (0.58 × 21% + 0.42 × 13% ≈ 17.6%, matching the overall 18%), so the table looks right and the text is wrong.
- The Android explanation (the deeper menu placement) therefore explains a pattern that doesn't exist. If anything, it predicts the opposite of what happened.
- This needs re-examination, not just a word swap. Why did iOS users, with the *shallower* path, drop more? Do iOS users rely more on Reorder? This matters for "targeting the fix", as you put it.

## Overstated claims

**3. "Nothing else changing" is not true of the removal.**
- v5.0 changed the tab bar, moved search, added a recipe feed *and* moved Reorder, so the fall on 2 February can't be pinned on Reorder alone.
- The isolated evidence is the *restoration* in v5.0.3, plus the support tickets and the 45% Reorder share. That evidence is fairly strong, but the "clean natural experiment" framing overstates it.
- Recovery was also incomplete (1.27 vs 1.28, and WAU still about 1,400 below baseline). That leaves room for a residual effect from the other changes.
- There is no seasonal check. A year-on-year comparison for February would help.

**4. The loss estimate is incomplete in the other direction too.**
- It stops at 23 February, but the weeks of 2 and 9 March were still below baseline (about 5,350 and 2,250 orders short).
- The roughly 4% WAU drop that hasn't fully recovered suggests some lasting customer loss that isn't counted.
- Conversely, some "lost" orders may simply have been deferred. The document should state its assumptions.

## The search-bar conclusion is unsupported and risky

**5. The "40% more orders" figure is correlational.**
- Customers who use search in a week are likely more engaged or have more purchase intent to begin with. This is classic selection bias.
- No pre-release comparison is given. Search existed before as a tab, so the relevant question is whether search usage or search-driven orders *increased*.
- "Search is clearly driving purchasing" is not supported by this evidence.

**6. The v5.2 plan repeats the v5.0 mistake.**
- Making search results the default landing view for *returning* users would displace the home screen. That is exactly where returning, frequent buyers access Reorder, which drives about 45% of orders.
- It is the same pattern this post-mortem diagnoses: changing a core flow for existing customers based on weak evidence.
- At minimum, it should go through actions 1 and 2 (existing-customer testing, staged rollout with a guardrail). Ideally it should be an A/B test before being described as a "clear direction".

## Gaps in detection and actions

**7. The four-week fix delay isn't analysed.**
- Escalation came on 10 February, but the fix shipped on 2 March.
- "The rollback decision was then delayed while we prepared a fix" is the single biggest driver of cost (roughly three weeks of about £420k/week), yet the document doesn't explain why.
- Missing details include who decided, what alternatives were considered, and why a revert wasn't possible. Action 4 helps, but the document should check whether reverting was technically feasible (e.g., app-store review, server-side flags).

**8. The actions are not "owned" as stated.**
- None of the four actions has an owner or a due date. Please add both.
- Smaller points:
  - Action 3's 5% week-on-week threshold would miss gradual declines. Consider a baseline-relative threshold as well.
  - Action 2's "used in more than 10% of orders" needs a defined data source so teams can actually apply it.
  - Daily monitoring would have caught this on 3 February. A weekly alert alone would only have fired around 9 February.

## Suggested corrections

| Item | Current | Should be |
|---|---|---|
| Lost revenue | ~£1.05m | ~£1.50m (state the window and assumptions) |
| Platform text | "concentrated among Android" | iOS declined more (−21% vs −13%); explanation needs revisiting |
| Root-cause framing | removal was a clean natural experiment | restoration provides the isolating evidence; removal coincided with other changes |
| Search finding | "clearly driving purchasing" | correlational; test before acting |
| v5.2 plan | search as default landing for returning users | subject to existing-customer testing and staged rollout, given Reorder risk |
